sections.body: A fallacy is a mistake in reasoning. It can make an argument sound convincing when it isn't. Spotting them protects you from being manipulated by ads, social media and even friends.
Bandwagon: 'Everyone's doing it, so it must be right.' Popularity doesn't prove something is true or good.
Straw man: twisting someone's argument into a weaker version, then attacking that. 'You want less homework? So you think school is pointless?'
False choice: pretending there are only two options when there are more. 'Either you're with us or against us.'
Attacking the person: criticising the speaker instead of their argument. 'Why listen to her about climate? She's only 14.'
Find one ad or online post this week that uses a fallacy. Which one is it?

quiz.q: 'Millions of people bought this energy drink, so it must be healthy.' Which fallacy?
hints: Does popularity prove something is healthy?
Example: 'This song has a billion views, so it's the best song ever' uses the same move.
quiz.explain: It uses popularity as proof, which is the bandwagon fallacy.

quiz.q: 'You don't want a phone ban in class? So you want students on TikTok all day!' Which fallacy?
hints: Is that what the person actually said?
The argument was changed into something more extreme.
Example: 'You want fewer cars downtown? So you hate cars!' twists the original view.
quiz.explain: It twists the original view into an extreme one that's easy to attack: a straw man.

quiz.q: 'Either we cancel the school trip or someone will get lost.' Why is this weak?
options: It ignores other options, like more supervision
hints: Are there really only two choices?
What else could the school do?
Example: 'Either you study all weekend or you'll fail' ignores studying a bit each day.
quiz.explain: It's a false choice. There are other options, like more adults or a buddy system.
